s: "No State shall… pass any… Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts."
The Marshall Court applied the clause vigorously.
It protected land grants (Fletcher v. Peck, 1810) and corporate charters (Dartmouth College, 1819), though it applied only to contracts already in existence (Ogden v. Saunders, 1827).
Home Building & Loan v. Blaisdell (1934) upheld a Depression-era mortgage moratorium, and the clause has been modest since.
Contracts Clause (Energy Reserves; Sveen v. Melin).
Does the state law operate as a substantial impairment of an existing contractual relationship?
Consider the extent to which it undermines the bargain, interferes with reasonable expectations, and prevents safeguarding of rights.
If so, does it serve a significant and legitimate public purpose, such as remedying a broad social or economic problem?
Is the adjustment reasonable and appropriate to that purpose?
When the state impairs its own contracts, scrutiny is stricter.
Courts defer less because the state's self-interest is at stake (U.S. Trust Co. v. New Jersey, 1977).
The clause limits only states and only retroactive impairment.
The federal government is constrained instead by due process.
